content: I'll start by reading the test image to analyze the visual symptoms.

This points to a stem/root disease causing sudden collapse: candidates include **Southern Blight**, **Bacterial Wilt**, **Southern Bacterial Wilt**, or **Sclerotinia Timber Rot**. Let me view one reference from each top candidate.

I've now used all 8 reference image views. Let me synthesize my findings.

**Summary of visual evidence:**

- **Test image**: Single tomato plant completely fallen/collapsed flat onto black plastic mulch. Plant appears to have failed at the stem near soil line. Leaves still partially green (not fully browned).

- **Southern Blight** (Bugwood_5): Shows tomato plants on plastic mulch with collapsed/dead plants — very similar field setting. Plants fallen over while still bearing fruit.

- **Southern Blight** (Bugwood_13): Shows tomato field on black plastic mulch with drooping/wilting foliage — same black mulch context.

- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot** (Bugwood_2): Shows plant on black plastic mulch with partial stem collapse, but collapse is higher up on the plant, not at soil line.

- **Bacterial Wilt** (Bugwood_6): Shows plants still standing/staked but wilted with dead foliage — plants not collapsed flat, different from test image.

**Conclusion**: The test image shows a complete whole-plant collapse lying flat on black plastic mulch, with the failure point at or near the soil line. This is the hallmark of **Southern Blight** (*Sclerotium rolfsii*), which causes rapid stem girdling at the soil line, leading to complete plant collapse while leaves may still retain some green color. The field setting (black plastic mulch, tomato) and the complete flat collapse pattern most closely match the Southern Blight references over Bacterial Wilt (which shows upright-but-wilted plants) or Sclerotinia (which collapses higher on the stem).
